name: Modality Effect
description: Immediate recall can change depending on whether information was heard or seen. In the classic list-memory version, spoken items often get an end-of-list memory advantage relative to visually presented items.
design_relevance_note: Design relevance is thin and narrow: mainly voice interfaces, spoken instructions, audio confirmations, IVR flows, and screen-reader-adjacent sequences. It is not honest to turn this into a broad 'audio is better than visual' product-design rule.
prevalence_note: Primarily a memory-lab term; it surfaces only occasionally in voice UX, accessibility, or multimodal-instruction design.

findings.description: Across immediate free recall and immediate serial recall tasks, auditory presentation improved recall at the end of the list relative to visual presentation, while longer lists also showed inverse early-list visual advantages. The paper treats these as common modality effects across both recall paradigms.
findings.source_title: Common modality effects in immediate free recall and immediate serial recall.
findings.source_venue: Journal of Experimental Psychology: Learning, Memory, and Cognition
